definition: Showing two versions of something (a page, an email, an ad) to different people at the same time to see which performs better. The winner becomes the new standard.
When people search using AI tools like ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, or Perplexity instead of Google. Businesses can now show up (or not) inside those AI answers.
A short description of an image added to the site's code. It helps visually impaired visitors and helps Google understand the picture.
The data that shows how people use your website — how many visitors, where they came from, what they clicked, and what they did.
The clickable words in a link. Good anchor text describes where the link goes (e.g. “our pricing page” rather than “click here”).
A link from another website to yours. Google treats backlinks a bit like recommendations — the more good ones you have, the more trusted your site looks.
The percentage of visitors who leave after seeing only one page. A very high bounce rate can mean the page didn't match what they were looking for.
The overall look, feel, and voice of your business — logo, colors, tone, messaging. It's how people recognize and remember you.
A few related services grouped together as one offer — usually easier to buy and often at a small discount vs picking each service on its own.
The one thing you want a visitor to do next — like “Book a Free Call” or “See Pricing.” Every good page has a clear CTA.
Creating useful articles, guides, videos, or posts that attract customers over time — instead of paying for ads.
When a visitor takes the action you wanted — filling out a form, buying, booking a call. Every campaign is measured by conversions.
The percentage of visitors who convert. If 100 people visit and 3 book a call, the conversion rate is 3%.
How much you pay each time someone clicks one of your ads.
How much you pay to have your ad shown a thousand times, whether or not people click.
A tool for keeping track of your leads and customers — who they are, what they've asked about, and what stage they're at in your pipeline.
Improving a website so more visitors take action — like booking a call or making a purchase.
The percentage of people who see something (an ad, an email, a search result) and actually click on it.
Your website address — like simplifiedstartup.com. Something you own and use across your website and email.
A score (out of 100) that estimates how strong a website looks to search engines. Higher usually means better ranking chances.
Sending emails to a list of customers or prospects — newsletters, offers, updates — to keep them engaged and drive sales.
Any action people take with your content — likes, comments, shares, replies. It's a sign your content is resonating.
Google's standard for good content: Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, and Trustworthiness. Sites that clearly show these tend to rank better.
The path someone takes from first hearing about you to becoming a customer — usually awareness, interest, decision, and action.
Optimizing your content so AI tools like ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, or Perplexity mention and recommend your business when people ask them questions.
Paid ads that appear at the top of Google search results. You pay per click.
A free tool from Google that shows you how visitors are using your website.
Your free business listing on Google — what people see on Google Maps and in local search results. Formerly Google My Business.
A word or phrase preceded by # on social media. It groups posts around a topic so people searching for that topic can find them.
The main page of your website — what people usually see first. Its job is to explain who you are and where to go next.
A single instance of your content or ad being shown to someone — whether or not they clicked or engaged.
Paying (or partnering with) someone who has a following on social media to promote your business to their audience.
Links from one page on your site to another. Helps visitors navigate and helps Google understand which pages are important.
A word or phrase people type into Google. SEO is largely about matching the keywords your customers use with the pages you create.
The work of finding out which keywords your customers actually search for, so your content targets the right ones.
The main numbers you use to measure success — like leads per month, cost per click, or search rankings.
A single page built for one specific purpose — usually to convert visitors from an ad or campaign into leads or customers.
Someone who has shown interest in your business — filled out a form, requested a quote, or booked a call.
The work of attracting people interested in your business and collecting their contact details so you can follow up.
The kind of SEO that helps a business show up on Google Maps and in local search results (e.g. “coffee shop near me”).
The short description of a page shown under its title in Google results. It doesn't affect ranking directly but does affect whether people click.
The clickable page title shown in Google search results. One of the most important SEO elements on any page.
A site that looks and works well on phones and tablets. Google prefers these, and most of your visitors are on mobile.
A page built around one specific service, business type, and location — like “SEO for realtors in Raleigh.” Designed to attract high-intent searches.
SEO work done off your own site — mainly earning backlinks and mentions from other trusted websites.
The percentage of people who open an email you send. A quick health check on your subject line and audience.
Visitors who come from Google's free (unpaid) search results — as opposed to paid ads or social.
A big all-in-one offer that covers many services together, usually at a lower price than buying each separately.
Ads shown in search results that you pay for — the top of Google, above the free results. Also called PPC or SEM.
Ads run on social media platforms like Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, or TikTok.
A paid advertising model where you only pay when someone clicks your ad. Google Ads and most social ads work this way.
Where your page appears in Google's results for a given keyword. Position 1 is the top, and higher is almost always better.
The number of unique people who saw your content — different from impressions, which count each view.
Ads shown to people who already visited your site — a reminder to come back and take the next step.
How much money you got back compared to how much you spent. A simple way to measure whether a campaign was worth it.
Extra code added to a page that helps Google understand what's on it — like reviews, prices, or FAQs. Often produces the “rich results” you see in search.
A broad term that usually means paid search ads on Google. Sometimes used to mean SEO + paid search together.
The work that helps a website show up higher in Google's free (unpaid) search results.
The page you see after typing something into Google. What appears where decides who gets clicked.
A file that lists all the pages on your site so Google can find and index them more easily.
The ongoing work of running a business's social accounts — posting, responding, and growing an audience.
The specific group of people your marketing is meant to reach — defined by things like age, location, industry, or interests.
The behind-the-scenes SEO work — site speed, mobile-friendliness, clean code, and structure — that makes Google trust and understand your site.
The number of people visiting your website, from all sources combined.
The web address of a page — like simplifiedstartup.com/services/seo. Clean, readable URLs are better for people and search engines.
How easy and pleasant a website is to use. Good UX keeps visitors around and helps them convert.
The visual and structural design of a website — how it looks, how it's laid out, and how visitors move through it.
Setting up your tools so repetitive tasks happen automatically — like follow-up emails, moving leads through your CRM, or posting to social media.
